newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Food aid trucks turn back from lawless Albania.
newsitem.headline: Food aid trucks turn back from lawless Albania.

text.p: Trucks ferrying international emergency food aid to Albania stopped at the Greek border on Thursday, fearing to cross to the strife-torn Balkan country's southern region where rebels and outlaw gangs rule.
It was the first attempt by the Geneva-based International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to send food aid into Albania by a land route.

Border police said the ICRC trucks, one with nine tonnes of food and one with technical gear, cleared Greek customs early on Thursday but waited all day for word from relief workers on the other side that it was safe to cross.
An ICRC spokesman in Tirana said the trucks would try to cross the border on Friday and hoped to make their way to the port of Durres, west of the capital, dropping off food in towns along the way.
The ICRC wants to secure a land route from Greece to supply Albania, which has been cut in two since an armed insurrection in the south early this month.

The first stop in Albania was to be the rebel stronghold of Gjirokaster, 30 km (20 miles) from the border. Rebel councils have imposed some order in the south but armed gangs still prey on residents and travellers.

Albania was swept by violence in January when a string of popular savings schemes collapsed, erasing millions of dollars. Rebels seized the south in March in an armed insurrection, blaming President Sali Berisha for the fiasco and demanding he quit.

Since then gangs have roamed the south, stealing, looting and killing. One person was killed and seven were wounded when gunmen attacked a bus near Tirana on Wednesday. Five policemen have been killed this week.
A number of countries, including six European Union states, want to get food and medical supplies safely into the shattered country of 3.4 million people as quickly as possible.
The emergency aid, relatively small in scale, and a foreign security force to oversee distribution are seen as essential to restoring order and paving the way to early elections in June.
In Vienna, Europe's top security body, the OSCE, noted some of its members wanted to set up the security force but said the U.N. Security Council should set out the appropriate mandate.
A 15-member European delegation met Prime Minister Bashkim Fino on Thursday to discuss the security force and elections which Berisha agreed to this month in a desperate bid to cling to power.
In his effort to ride out the storm, Berisha also appointed Fino, an opposition Socialist, to oversee a unity government -- something that he had vowed for weeks not to do.
"There is general recognition in Europe that we can't do anything in Albania unless security improves," Dutch diplomat and European group leader Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg told reporters.
He said Fino and other ministers had agreed that a foreign security force was necessary and said Fino had requested early assistance in overseeing fair elections this summer.
Asked about force numbers, he said: "If you want to do it really seriously, you need around 3,000 people. We are talking about police, gendarmes or military police of some sort."
Six EU states -- France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece and Austria -- have military experts in Albania to prepare for the security force. Turkey and Romania have also offered to assist.
D'Ansembourg said Fino had asked for help from the OSCE -- the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe -- to ensure fair elections. Fino wanted the OSCE to arrive in April.
Berisha, whom d'Ansembourg will meet on Friday , has been less keen on OSCE observers since they accused his Democrats of staging badly flawed national elections last May.

Albania's police and army disintegrated in the face of the armed uprising and defence ministry officials told d'Ansembourg the strength of the army, the officer corps and conscripts, was now 15,000 compared to around 50,000 before the revolt.
D'Ansembourg's team includes experts from the 54-nation OSCE, the 15-nation EU and its executive Commission and the 40-nation Council of Europe.
